newsitem.title: CHINA: Visa looks to boost China credit card business.
newsitem.headline: Visa looks to boost China credit card business.

text.p: The number of Visa cards on issue in China hit 12 million by the end of 1996, but the vast majority of Chinese still have no way to access credit with their plastic, Visa International officials said on Tuesday.
The global credit card group was keen to be part of the development of China's credit infrastructure, Visa International President Edmund Jensen told a news conference in Beijing.

"Our core commitment is to continue to help, especially with the prospective 'Golden Card' project," Jensen said in a reference to Beijing's plan for the popularisation of the use of electronic money in China's booming urban areas.

The number of Visa cards on issue in China soared to 11 million by the end of June last year, up by 85 percent compared with a year before. The number of cards rose further to 12 million by the end of 1996, company officials said.
But about 99 percent of the Visa cards on issue in China were still simple debit cards, they said.
Visa was working with the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China to sell some "true" credit cards, they said.

Economists say the development of personal credit in China has been hampered by weak infrastructure, a high savings rate and the absence of any way to reliably calculate credit risk among urban residents with no history of borrowing.
Visa's China business was being subsidised by other more mature markets, with little chance of profitability until card service infrastructure was put in place, Visa officials said.
"We made quite an investment (in China) because, as you know, for a payment system to be developed, infrastructure comes first," Jensen said.
Visa would continue to invest in China and other developing countries, he said but gave no details.

Because China had no existing electronic credit network, Beijing could probably leapfrog toward more efficient and effective technologies in the future, he said, adding that the potential for growth was huge.
China could have more credit cards than any other national market in seven to 10 years, he said.

Visa had built gateways to its international network in Beijing, Shanghai, southern Guangzhou and booming Shenzhen near the border with Hong Kong and was working with the central bank to build a national system, company officials said.
As the national system developed, increasing numbers of Visa cards issued in China were expected to be used internationally, they said.
Visa currently has 10 member banks in China, including major state banks and commercial banks that jointly issue cards.
